BEFORE THE
                           FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


           In the Matter of the Application of:      )
                                                     )
           DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC         )      Project No. P-15424-000



               NEW ENGLAND FISHERMEN’S STEWARDSHIP ASSOCIATION
                                     MOTION TO INTERVENE

    Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or the
“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, the New England Fishermen’s Stewardship
Association (“NEFSA”) moves to intervene in the proceeding regarding the DeepGreen Western
Passage SPV LLC (“DeepGreen”) preliminary permit application for the proposed DeepGreen
Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub (“Project”)1. By this motion, the NEFSA
seeks to ensure that recovering and economically crucial fisheries are protected as FERC evaluates
the application.

                                    CONTACT INFORMATION

   All filings, orders, and correspondence respecting these proceedings and this intervention
should be sent to:
      David E. Frulla
      Kelley Drye & Warren LLP
      670 Maine Avenue SW, Suite 600
      Washington, DC 20024
      (202) 342-8648
      DFrulla@KelleyDrye.com

      I.       DESCRIPTION OF INTERVENOR
    NEFSA is a non-profit, non-partisan advocacy organization formed under the laws of the State
of Maine, representing approximately 900 licensed commercial fishermen and lobstermen.
Members of NEFSA harvest in the Western Passage and adjacent waters of Passamaquoddy Bay
and Cobscook Bay, Washington County, Maine. NEFSA’s mission focuses on promoting healthy
fish stocks, sustaining the livelihoods of fishermen, and preserving the region’s fishing heritage.



1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.214.


Motion to Intervene – 1
      NEFSA and its members may be adversely impacted by the outcome of this proceeding. Rule
214(b)(2) requires a movant to state its interest in sufficient factual detail to demonstrate that it has
or represents an interest which may be directly affected by the outcome of the proceeding, or that
its participation is in the public interest. NEFSA satisfies both standards.
    NEFSA's members fish for herring, scallops and urchin, and set lobster gear within and
immediately adjacent to the area DeepGreen proposes to study for a docking cradle, thirty-four
subsea compute pods, a tidal-sensing power platform, up to sixteen 300-kW hydrokinetic turbines,
and a 1.5-mile hybrid power-and-fiber subsea cable. NEFSA fishermen live in Washington
County, Maine, and reside in Eastport, Pembroke, Perry, Robbinston and Dennysville. Those
fishermen will be directly affected by DeepGreen as they prosecute the lobster, scallop, urchin and
herring fishery. Washington County averages over $100 million dollars per year in fishery landings
from 2001-2025.2 Issuance of a preliminary permit would confer on DeepGreen priority to seek a
license for development directly on these grounds, and the studies conducted under the permit will
define the record on which any license decision will rest. NEFSA members’ economic,
operational, and navigational interests therefore may be directly affected by the outcome of this
proceeding.
    NEFSA’s participation is further in the public interest because they possess first-hand, site-
specific knowledge of bottom conditions, tidal currents, gear deployment patterns, vessel traffic,
and seasonal fishing activity in the Western Passage that will assist the Commission in developing
a complete record.3

    II.     THE PROPOSED PROJECT
    DeepGreen filed an application for a preliminary permit under section 4(f) of the Federal Power
Act ("FPA") on February 11, 2026, supplemented and amended on June 8 and July 30, 2026. The
permit would allow DeepGreen to study the feasibility of the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-
Compute & Infrastructure Hub, Project No. 15424-000, in the Western Passage of the Bay of
Fundy near Eastport, Maine. FERC’s Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted for
Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions to Intervene, and Competing Applications is dated
August 19, 2026 and was published August 25, 2026.4
    At the preliminary-permit stage, parties are entitled to conduct surveys and studies to prepare
for pilot and commercial stages of development. Subsequent development would result in up to 10
to 15 megawatts of electricity generation from up to 34 tidal turbines, powering sub-surface data
center infrastructure. The Project is thus not a conventional hydrokinetic facility. Its principal
purpose appears to be the siting of industrial computing infrastructure on the seabed, with tidal
generation serving that load. That novel combination—and its potential to expand roughly fifteen-

Motion to Intervene – 2
 fold in footprint—warrants close scrutiny of its effects on the marine environment and on existing,
long-established uses of these waters, including commercial fishing.

    III.     GROUNDS FOR INTERVENTION

    As noted above, and in conformity with FERC Rule 214, NEFSA has and represents interests
that may be directly affected by the outcome of the proceeding, and that its participation in these
proceedings is in the public interest.5 The Project’s preliminary surveys, the placement of turbines,
data-center pods, and a 1.5-mile export cable, and any associated exclusion or safety zones would
directly affect where, when, and whether NEFSA’s members may fish.

    Other movants have sought intervention to protect marine wildlife and their habitats. While
NEFSA shares this interest in healthy marine ecosystems, no other party represents the
commercial, navigational, and economic interests of the working fishermen whose livelihoods
depend on continued access to these grounds. NEFSA brings first-hand, on-the-water knowledge
of fishing activity, gear placement, seasonal patterns, and local oceanographic conditions that will
assist FERC in developing a complete administrative record.

             a. Environmental and Ecological Risks to Marine Habitats and Fisheries

    Western Passage is a biologically productive, high-current marine environment connected to
the Bay of Fundy. Its tidal flows concentrate plankton and forage species that support
commercially important fish stocks and migratory species. The Project threatens these resources
at every stage, beginning with the surveys proposed for the preliminary-permit term and escalating
with construction and operation of the pilot and commercial phases.

     Underwater noise is among the most immediate of these threats at the Project’s initial stage.
DeepGreen’s proposed high-resolution bathymetric and geophysical surveys would introduce
echosounder, sonar, and other survey-equipment noise into the passage, and later turbine
installation, vessel traffic, and operation of turbines and data-center pods would add sustained
construction and operational noise. Fish rely on sound to locate prey, avoid predators, navigate,
and coordinate spawning, and many commercially important species—including cod, haddock,
and herring—are sensitive to low-frequency sound.6 A recent systematic review of the scientific
literature published in Marine Pollution Bulletin examined biological responses to underwater
noise across marine taxa and developed taxon-informed ranges of noise levels at which behavioral,
physiological, and physical effects occur.7 This review found that anthropogenic noise can cause
fish to abandon habitat, alter schooling and vertical distribution, disrupt spawning aggregations,

Motion to Intervene – 3
 elevate stress hormones, mask acoustic communication, and, at high exposures, cause hearing loss
and tissue injury. Invertebrates central to New England fisheries, such as lobster and scallops, have
shown behavioral and physiological responses to seismic and other impulsive sounds. For
NEFSA’s members, these effects translate directly into displaced fish, reduced catchability, and
impaired recruitment in the grounds they fish.

    The Project would also physically disturb the seabed. Survey activities, turbine and pod
foundations, and placement or trenching of the 1.5-mile export cable may disturb or destroy the
sensitive benthic habitat used for spawning, nursery, and foraging by groundfish, lobster, scallops,
and other species crucial to the Maine fishery. Expansion to as much as 400 acres in Phase 2 of
the Project would multiply that disturbance.

    Finally, the tidal turbines themselves may injure or kill fish through heat, collisions and
entrapment, and may impede the movement of migratory species that pass through Passamaquoddy
Bay. Widescale extraction of energy from Western Passage’s tidal flows, particularly at the scale
contemplated in Phase 2 of the Project, may also impact current velocity, sedimentation, and
nutrient mixing—the very processes that sustain the area’s productivity and the fisheries that
depend on it.8

             b. Economic Harm to Commercial Fishing Operations and Fishing-Dependent
                Communities

    The communities that make up the Washington county shoreline are among the most fishing-
dependent in New England. The Project threatens economic harm to these communities in several
respects: (1) loss of access to fishing grounds within the Project footprint, cable corridor, and any
safety or exclusion zones; (2) gear loss and conflicts from survey vessels and subsea structures;
(3) increased fuel and transit costs where vessels must navigate around Project infrastructure in a
constrained, high-current passage; (4) reduced catch rates if fish are displaced by noise, heat, or
habitat alteration; and (5) downstream harm to processors, dealers, bait suppliers, boatyards, and
other shoreside businesses that depend on local landings. These harms will fall disproportionately
on small, family-owned operations that have limited ability to relocate, and which make up a
substantial portion of NEFSA’s membership.

    Further yet, Western Passage is a narrow, heavily used waterway, and its fishing grounds have
been worked by local families for generations. The Project would site industrial computing
infrastructure in this constrained space, with potential expansion from 27.1 acres to as much as
400 acres. The record does not yet demonstrate why subsea data-center pods—whose function is
unrelated to the marine environment—must be located on productive fishing grounds rather than
on land or in less sensitive locations. FERC should require DeepGreen to evaluate siting

Motion to Intervene – 4
 alternatives, minimize the Project footprint, and avoid areas of documented fishing activity before
any study plan or further authorization advances.

    More broadly, NEFSA wishes to emphasize that the Project is not being developed in isolation.
The Gulf of Maine and Bay of Fundy are subject to accelerating ocean-use pressures, including
proposed and existing tidal energy projects, offshore wind leasing and transmission, aquaculture
expansion, shipping, and fishery management closures for protected species. Each incremental
loss of fishing grounds compounds the last. NEFSA urges FERC to require a robust cumulative-
impact analysis addressing fishery resources, protected species, habitat, and fishing-community
socioeconomics across both phases of the Project and in combination with other reasonably
foreseeable activities.

   IV.     STATEMENT OF POSITION
   NEFSA seeks to intervene in this proceeding to ensure that the interests of the fishing
communities are protected, as well as the fisheries that provide an economic lifeline to these
communities, and dinner for countless Americans. NEFSA further seeks to ensure that the project
comports with all applicable state and federal laws.
    NEFSA opposes issuance of the preliminary permit due to the concerns raised above about the
Project’s potential environmental impacts on the scallop, lobster, herring and urchin fisheries off
the coast of Maine, and the economic impacts that intruding on these fisheries may cause. If FERC
chooses to issue a preliminary permit, NEFSA respectfully asks that DeepGreen be required to
consult with NEFSA, NOAA Fisheries, and the Maine Department of Marine Resources in
developing its study plan, and be required to provide periodic progress reports to these entities

   V.       CONCLUSION
   Because NEFSA has substantial interests in this proceeding, and in the Project’s potential
economic and ecological impacts on the Maine fishing industry, intervention is necessary for
NEFSA to represent those interests and to prevent harm. These interests are not represented by
any other party in the proceeding. As such, and for the foregoing reasons, NEFSA respectfully
requests that FERC grant this Motion to Intervene in the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-
Compute & Infrastructure Hub, Project No. P-15424-000.
